topic: Choosing optimistic versus pessimistic locking for concurrent updates
tomorrowTopic: Diagnosing a lost-update bug in a concurrent REST update

hook.headline: Choose conflicts or blocking deliberately
hook.hook: Optimistic and pessimistic locking solve overlapping concurrency problems, but they move the cost to different parts of the request lifecycle.
hook.visualCaption: Optimistic locking detects conflicting writes; pessimistic locking reserves database access earlier.
hook.microExample: rare conflicts → version check; hot row → consider database lock

mentalModel.title: Where should contention surface?
mentalModel.coreIdea: With a versioned JPA entity, optimistic locking detects conflicting updates when the provider checks the version. Pessimistic locking requests a database-level lock earlier, so competing transactions may wait instead of progressing to a later conflict.
mentalModel.keyOutcome: Choose based on contention, retry cost and how harmful blocking would be.
mentalModel.mentalShortcut: contention → retry cost → lock duration → strategy

code.title: Version the shared state
code.intro: A JPA version attribute gives the provider a value for detecting conflicting entity updates.
code.highlightReason: The version value lets the persistence provider detect that another transaction changed the entity since this state was read.
code.takeaway: Optimistic locking works well when conflicts are uncommon and failed work can be retried or rejected cleanly.
code.professionalNote: A pessimistic lock is requested explicitly, for example with LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE; exact SQL and lock behaviour are provider and database dependent.

production.title: A hot inventory row
production.scenario: Many checkout requests update the same inventory record. Optimistic locking avoids holding a lock during normal processing, but frequent conflicts now cause repeated retries and wasted application work.
problems: High contention can make optimistic retries expensive or user-visible.
Pessimistic locking can reduce conflicting progress but introduces waiting and possible deadlocks.
production.professionalApproach: Measure conflict frequency and transaction duration first. Prefer optimistic locking for low contention; consider a short pessimistic critical section when contention is predictably high and serialized access is acceptable.
production.debugClue: Frequent optimistic-lock failures on one record indicate contention; long lock waits after switching indicate the opposite cost has surfaced.

interview.question: When would you choose optimistic locking over pessimistic locking for a JPA update path?
interview.answer: I prefer optimistic locking when concurrent writes to the same entity are relatively uncommon and retrying or rejecting a conflict is acceptable. Pessimistic locking is more attractive when contention is predictably high and duplicated work is expensive, but I keep the transaction short because database locks can create waits and deadlocks.
